beats.text: In 1964 two Bell Labs engineers could not get rid of a hiss.
beats.note: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson were using a 20 foot horn antenna at Holmdel. After allowing for the sky and their equipment, 3.5 K of noise was left.

beats.text: They checked everything, including the pigeons.
beats.note: They removed pigeons nesting in the antenna and cleaned out the droppings. The noise remained.

beats.context: How much more intense the signal was than they had expected, according to the National Historic Landmark nomination.

beats.text: Princeton physicists were about to go looking for it.
beats.note: Robert Dicke's group, about 60 km away, was preparing to search for this radiation. Penzias heard of a related preprint from his friend Bernard Burke, then called Dicke.

beats.text: Both teams published together in July 1965.
beats.note: Penzias and Wilson's short paper ran in Astrophysical Journal Letters straight after the Princeton paper.

beats.text: They won the 1978 Nobel Prize in Physics.
beats.note: Half went to Penzias and Wilson jointly for the discovery. The other half went to Pyotr Kapitsa.

beats.text: A noise they could not remove turned out to be the discovery.
